It calculates the surviving radiance along a ray segment in an absorption-only medium where no scattering or emission occurs [S2, unofficial][S3, book].

Both Source [S2] and Source [S3] explicitly define absorption as the attenuation of radiance where particles absorb energy (converting it to other forms like heat) without mentioning scattering or emission in the context of the absorption-only calculation. They provide the differential equation $dL = -σ_a L dt$ and the integral solution for surviving radiance $L_{surviving} = L_{initial} e^{-∫σ_a dt}$, which mathematically represents the calculation of surviving radiance in a medium where only absorption occurs (no scattering or emission). The claim accurately reflects the content of both sources.

- Input: Incident radiance $L_i$ at the start of the segment, the absorption coefficient field $\sigma_a(p, \omega)$, the start position $p$, the direction $\omega$, and the segment length $d$ [S2, unofficial][S3, book].

The claim lists specific inputs required to determine the effect of absorption on radiance: incident radiance ($L_i$), absorption coefficient field ($σ_a$), start position ($p$), direction ($ω$), and segment length ($d$). Source [S3] explicitly defines the differential change in radiance as $d L_o = -σ_a(p, ω) L_i(p, -ω) dt$, involving $L_i$, $σ_a$, $p$, $ω$, and $dt$ (distance). It further provides the integrated solution for surviving radiance over a distance $d$ starting at $p$ in direction $ω$, which depends on all these variables. Source [S2] similarly derives the attenuation formula using $L(p,w)$, $σ_a(p,w)$, $p$, $w$, and $d$. Therefore, all facts in the claim are present and supported by the evidence.
